extractions.quote: Abstract—A 43-year-old woman presented with clinical and electrophysiologic features of stiff person syndrome (SPS), without abdominal or lumbar paraspinal muscle involvement. Investigations revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma of the lung with positive anti-Ri antibodies. Her clinical condition improved with diazepam, baclofen, tizanidine, and palliative chemotherapy. Screening for an underlying malignancy and anti-Ri antibodies should be considered in patients with SPS when clinical presentation is atypical.
A 43-year-old right-handed woman had noted transient pins and needles and generalized upper limb weakness after waking, 15 months prior to referral to our hospital for further investigation.

Clinical assessment over the following 3 months revealed that her dysarthria and dysphagia stabilized, the upper limb and cervicothoracic muscle stiffness and spasms improved, and although she was more mobile, she required considerable assistance with activities of daily living.

However, in contrast to patients with SPS associated with anti-GAD antibodies, she had mild dysarthria and dysphagia, prominent upper limb and cervical paraspinal muscle involvement, and sparing of abdominal and lumbar paraspinal muscles. In addition, there was mild leg spasticity with flexor plantar responses, suggesting reticulospinal tract overactivity. The multifocal nature of the disorder, in association with brainstem symptoms, and negative anti-GAD and -amphiphysin I antibodies, raises the possibility of an evolving progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity.
